name: DO THE CREMINI, DO THE THYME BURGER

recipe.history:
Cremini mushrooms — Agaricus bisporus in their brown-capped, immature form — are the same species as the white button mushroom and, when allowed to mature further, the portobello. This single species, with its remarkable range from small and mild to large and deeply savory depending on age and color, is now the most commercially cultivated mushroom in the world. The species is native to grasslands across North America and Europe, where it grows naturally in meadows and fields from late summer through autumn. Large-scale cultivation began in France in the seventeenth century, when French gardeners discovered that they could grow mushrooms year-round in the cool, humidity-controlled tunnels of limestone caves near Paris — the champignons de Paris that remain a staple of French cuisine to this day. The brown cremini variety, sometimes marketed under the Italian-sounding name 'Baby Bella,' was largely displaced by the white button variety through most of the twentieth century because American consumers preferred the cleaner visual presentation of the white mushroom, even though the cremini possesses a noticeably deeper, more complex, earthier flavor. Thyme, a Mediterranean herb from the mint family, has been the mushroom's most faithful culinary companion across every European cooking tradition — the two were made for each other, the herbal resin of the thyme highlighting the umami depth of the mushroom.

Cremini mushrooms and their close relatives entered American restaurant cooking as a fine-dining staple through classical French cuisine influence, but the mushroom burger — the concept of sautéed mushrooms as a burger topping rather than a side dish — is thoroughly American in its casual, generous excess. It became ubiquitous on bar menus and diner specials through the 1980s and 1990s, typically as sautéed button or cremini mushrooms piled high over a patty with Swiss cheese, under the designation 'mushroom Swiss' — one of the great humble American burger configurations. The gourmet burger movement of the 2000s elevated this combination by treating the mushrooms with more care: dry-sautéed over high heat rather than steamed in butter, finished with fresh thyme and a deglaze of dry sherry or white wine, allowed to develop the deep, meaty, almost stock-like flavor they achieve when properly handled.

I have burned more mushrooms trying to do the right thing than I care to admit. The right thing, with creminis, is to get the pan genuinely hot — not medium, not medium-high, but hot — and add the mushrooms to a dry pan with no fat at first, spreading them in a single layer and leaving them completely alone for two to three minutes. This is the hardest part, because every instinct says to stir them, to move them, to make sure they're not burning. But if you leave them alone in a properly hot dry pan they will release their liquid, that liquid will evaporate, and what remains will be concentrated and brown and extraordinary in a way that gently sweated mushrooms can never be. The first time I did this correctly — actually left them alone long enough — the smell when I finally stirred them was something I have been trying to reproduce in every kitchen I've worked in since.

The medium-rare burger — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — and cremini mushrooms have a relationship built on umami sympathy. Mushrooms are loaded with glutamates, the same amino acids responsible for the savory depth perception we call umami, and the beef in a medium-rare patty has retained enough of its own glutamate-rich juices that the two produce a genuinely synergistic amplification of savoriness on the palate. The mushroom's earthiness lifts the mineral qualities of the medium-rare beef; the beef's pink juices enrich the concentrated mushroom fond on the bun. Overcook the patty to well done, strip it of its juices and its gelatin, and the mushrooms are left without a partner — they are alone in the burger, which is one of the saddest configurations in cooking. Medium rare keeps everyone in the conversation.
ingredients: 2 large eggs (1 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves, finely chopped
1 1/2 lbs cremini mushrooms, cleaned and sliced 1/4-inch thick
1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves (plus extra sprigs for cooking)
2 tablespoons dry sherry or dry white wine
1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves, finely chopped
2 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves, finely minced
Kosher salt and white pepper to taste
Extra virgin olive oil for finishing
instructions: 1. MAKE THE THYME-BUTTER ROLLS — DAY BEFORE: Combine warm milk, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.
2. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, 1 egg, softened butter, and chopped thyme. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes, then increase to medium and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate overnight. Alternatively, allow to rise at room temperature 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled, then proceed.

4. Divide dough into 6 equal portions. Shape into tight round balls. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 1 to 2 hours if working from refrigerated dough (or 45 minutes from room temperature risen dough).
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 15 to 17 minutes until golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

6. MAKE THE THYME-DIJON AIOLI: Whisk egg yolks, both mustards, and garlic paste in a medium bowl. Stream in neutral oil very slowly, whisking constantly, until the emulsion thickens. Stream in olive oil. Whisk in lemon juice. Fold in minced thyme and chives. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

7. SAUTÉ THE CREMINI MUSHROOMS: Heat a large wide skillet — cast iron is ideal — over high heat until very hot. Add mushrooms in a single layer (work in two batches if needed) to a completely dry pan. Do not add any fat. Leave completely undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes until the mushrooms release their liquid and begin to brown on the bottom.

8. Stir and continue cooking 2 to 3 minutes more until mushrooms are deeply golden brown and the pan is mostly dry again. Push mushrooms to the side. Reduce heat to medium. Add butter, olive oil, garlic, and thyme sprigs to the empty side of the pan. Let the butter foam and the garlic sizzle 60 seconds.

9. Toss mushrooms with the garlic-butter mixture. Add sherry or white wine and soy sauce. Stir and cook 2 minutes until the liquid is absorbed. Season with salt and pepper. Remove thyme sprigs. Stir in chopped parsley. Set aside and keep warm.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground short rib. Season with salt, pepper, and thyme. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
11. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes first side for a deep crust.

12. Flip once. Lay a slice of Gruyère over each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
13. TOAST THE ROLLS: Split rolls and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds until golden.
14. ASSEMBLE: Spread thyme-Dijon aioli generously on both cut sides of the roll. Place baby spinach or watercress on the bottom bun. Add the rested, Gruyère-topped patty.
15. Pile the sautéed cremini mushrooms generously over the patty — be lavish here, mushrooms compress when eaten and more is always more. Drape a few shavings of Parmesan over the mushrooms.
16. Drizzle lightly with extra virgin olive oil and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top roll and serve immediately.
